overview:
“Khamemi savva jive” (Prakrit: खामेमि सव्वे जीवे / khāmemi savve jīve) is one of the most widely recited Jain forgiveness formulas and forms the opening line of a short prayer that encapsulates the Jain ethic of universal non‑violence, friendship, and the renunciation of enmity. The full verse is usually given as: “Khamemi savva jīve, savve jīvā khamantu me, metti me savva‑bhūesu, veram majjha na kenai.” In many communities it is recited together with the phrase “Micchāmi dukkadam,” especially during the annual Paryuṣaṇ / Samvatsarī observances and in daily pratikramaṇa (ritual of repentance and introspection).

Linguistically, the formula is in Jaina Prakrit. “Khamemi” is a first‑person singular verb meaning “I forgive”; “savva” means “all”; “jīve” means “living beings.” The subsequent lines shift from granting forgiveness to requesting it, affirming universal friendship, and renouncing hostility. A commonly accepted translation of the whole verse is: “I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all beings; I have enmity with none.” This simple structure expresses a bilateral movement of forgiveness—outward from the practitioner to all beings, and inward from all beings to the practitioner—grounded in the Jain view that every jīva (soul) is intrinsically worthy of respect.

In practice, “Khamemi savva jive” functions as a condensed ethical and spiritual declaration. During Samvatsarī (the principal forgiveness day), Jains approach relatives, friends, colleagues, and even strangers with the greeting “Micchāmi dukkadam,” often implicitly or explicitly framed by the “Khamemi savva jive” verse. The practitioner acknowledges that harm may have been done knowingly or unknowingly through thought, speech, or action, and seeks to dissolve the karmic consequences of such harm by repentance and forgiveness. The verse is also recited at the close of many religious activities (such as scriptural recitation or temple worship) as a way of asking forgiveness for any errors in performance and reaffirming non‑violence and goodwill toward all beings.

Doctrinally, the prayer is closely tied to the Jain vows of ahiṃsā (non‑violence), aparigraha (non‑possessiveness), and the broader discipline of pratikramaṇa. By forgiving and seeking forgiveness from “all living beings,” the practitioner recognizes the vast range of jīvas—from one‑sensed organisms to five‑sensed beings—and the subtle ways in which violence can occur. The verse does not function as a mechanical erasure of karma; rather, traditional teaching presents it as an expression of genuine inner transformation: the abandonment of anger, resentment, and hostility, and the cultivation of maitri (friendship) and karuṇā (compassion). In this sense, “Khamemi savva jive” is both a liturgical formula and a lifelong ethical aspiration.

Historically and ritually, the verse appears in different liturgical contexts across Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions, often as part of the “Tikhuto” or “Kṣamāpath” (forgiveness text) recited at the end of pratikramaṇa or other rites. Community education materials emphasize that the verse is not limited to human relationships: it extends to all forms of life, including insects and micro‑organisms, reflecting the Jain cosmology in which every living being is a soul journeying through saṃsāra. Modern expositions also connect the practice of reciting “Khamemi savva jive” with psychological and social benefits—reducing conflict, fostering reconciliation, and encouraging humility—while insisting that its primary significance remains spiritual: aligning one’s conduct with the path to liberation (mokṣa) through the purification of karma.

Because the formula is short and easily memorized, it is taught to children and new learners as a gateway into Jain ethics. At the same time, advanced practitioners and scholars read it in light of more technical doctrines such as the guṇasthānas (stages of spiritual development) and the analysis of passions (kaṣāyas). From this perspective, sincerely living the meaning of “Khamemi savva jive” is one way of weakening anger, pride, deceit, and greed, thereby allowing the soul’s innate qualities of knowledge and perception to shine forth. The verse thus bridges everyday interpersonal practice and the deeper metaphysical aims of Jainism.

It is important to note that there is no single canonical “author” of this formula in the way that a philosophical treatise might have an identifiable composer. Rather, it is embedded in liturgical traditions and transmitted through monastic lineages and community practice. Different editions and recensions may vary slightly in spelling or phonetic detail, and translations can differ in nuance (for example, “enmity” versus “hostility,” “friendship” versus “amity”). Nonetheless, the core meaning—universal forgiveness, mutual reconciliation, and the renunciation of hatred—remains consistent across sects and languages.

primary_sources.title: Forgiveness prayer (often called Tikhuto / Kṣamāpath in liturgical use)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous liturgical tradition; transmitted in Jain monastic and lay practice
primary_sources.original_text: खामेमि सव्वजीवे सव्वेजीवा खमंतु मे। मित्ती मे सव्वभुएसु वेरं मज्झ न केणई॥
primary_sources.transliteration: Khamemi savva jīve, savve jīvā khamantu me, metti me savva‑bhūesu, veram majjha na kenai.
primary_sources.translation: I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all beings; I have enmity with none.
primary_sources.notes: This short Prakrit verse is widely used in Śvetāmbara and Digambara liturgies as a prayer of universal forgiveness. It is commonly recited at the end of pratikramaṇa (ritual repentance and introspection), during Samvatsarī (the principal forgiveness day), and after many religious activities to seek forgiveness for any errors in performance and to reaffirm non‑violence and goodwill toward all beings. The wording may appear with minor orthographic variations across different prayer books and regional traditions, but the structure and meaning remain consistent: unilateral forgiveness, bilateral seeking of forgiveness, affirmation of universal friendship, and renunciation of hostility.

primary_sources.title: Tikhuto prayer with Micchāmi Dukkadam
primary_sources.author: Anonymous liturgical tradition; embedded in Jain ritual manuals
primary_sources.original_text: मिच्छामि दुक्कडं। खामेमि सव्वजीवे सव्वेजीवा खमंतु मे। मित्ती मे सव्वभुएसु वेरं मज्झ न केणई॥
primary_sources.transliteration: Micchāmi dukkadaṃ. Khamemi savva jīve, savve jīvā khamantu me, metti me savva‑bhūesu, veram majjha na kenai.
primary_sources.translation: May all the evil that has been done be fruitless. I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all beings; I have enmity with none.
primary_sources.notes: In many ritual contexts, especially Samvatsarī and other major pratikramaṇa observances, the forgiveness verse is preceded by the phrase “Micchāmi dukkadaṃ,” traditionally glossed as “May the bad deeds be rendered ineffective” or “May all the evil that has been done be fruitless.” Together, these lines form a compact act of repentance and forgiveness: acknowledging past wrongs, seeking their karmic neutralization, forgiving all beings, and renouncing enmity. Community education materials and modern commentaries often present this combined formula as the heart of Jain forgiveness practice.

misconceptions.myth: “Khamemi savva jive” is only about forgiving human beings, especially friends and relatives.
misconceptions.reality: The Prakrit term “savva jīve” explicitly refers to all living beings, not just humans. Traditional explanations emphasize that the verse extends to every jīva—from one‑sensed organisms to five‑sensed beings—reflecting the Jain doctrine that all life is worthy of respect. Limiting the prayer to human relationships misses its cosmological and ethical scope, which includes insects, animals, plants, and micro‑organisms.

misconceptions.myth: Reciting “Khamemi savva jive” automatically erases all bad karma, regardless of one’s inner state or future conduct.
misconceptions.reality: Jain teachings present the verse as part of pratikramaṇa, which requires genuine remorse, introspection, and a commitment to change. Merely repeating the words without inner transformation is not described as a mechanical cancellation of karma. The prayer supports karmic purification when it is accompanied by sincere repentance, forgiveness, and a practical effort to reduce violence and hostility in thought, speech, and action.

misconceptions.myth: “Khamemi savva jive” is a sect‑specific formula belonging only to one Jain tradition (for example, only Śvetāmbara or only Digambara).
misconceptions.reality: While liturgical details and pronunciation can vary, the forgiveness verse is widely attested across major Jain traditions and is closely associated with shared practices such as Samvatsarī, Kṣamāvaṇī (Forgiveness Day), and pratikramaṇa. Different communities may embed it in distinct ritual frameworks or pair it with other sutras, but the core meaning of universal forgiveness and renunciation of enmity is recognized across sectarian lines.

misconceptions.myth: The verse is a purely social custom with no deeper doctrinal significance.
misconceptions.reality: Although “Khamemi savva jive” has important social effects—reconciliation, reduction of conflict, and strengthening of relationships—it is rooted in central Jain doctrines: ahiṃsā (non‑violence), the analysis of karma, and the recognition of every jīva’s intrinsic worth. Traditional commentaries and modern expositions link the sincere practice of this prayer to the weakening of passions (kaṣāyas) and progress on the path toward liberation (mokṣa), not merely to social harmony.
